questiontext.text:
To prove a statement by contradiction, you start by assuming that it is false.

Statement: {@stmtxt@}.

Complete the assumption that starts a proof by contradiction of this statement. Type \(\leq\) as <= and \(\geq\) as >=.

Assume that the inequality [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] holds for [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] of {@domtxt@}.

generalfeedback.text:
The statement says that {@dtorig@} holds for every choice of {@domtxt@}. It is false exactly when at least one choice fails it, that is, gives {@dtarel@}. So the proof starts: assume that there is at least one choice of {@domtxt@} for which {@dtarel@}.

Two things change. ‘For every’ becomes ‘for at least one’, and the inequality is replaced by its opposite: \(\geq\) becomes \(\lt\), \(\gt\) becomes \(\leq\), \(\leq\) becomes \(\gt\), and \(\lt\) becomes \(\geq\). Any rearrangement of {@dtarel@} is also correct, for example {@dtalt@}.

Two slips to avoid. Assuming that {@dtarel@} holds for every choice is far too strong: one failing choice is enough to make the statement false. And [[if test='tstrict']]{@dtnear@} includes the case where the two sides are equal, which agrees with the statement[[else]]{@dtnear@} leaves out the case where the two sides are equal, in which the statement is false[[/if]], so it is not the opposite of {@dtorig@}.

questionnote.text: Variant {@vnum@}: assume at least one choice with {@dtarel@}

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Examples 8.6 and 8.7 (pp. 41-42) in Section 8 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

node.description: At least one choice, opposite inequality

truefeedback.text: Correct: the statement is false exactly when at least one choice gives {@dtarel@}.
That says the same as the statement you want to prove. A proof by contradiction starts from the opposite: that the statement is false.

node.description: Diagnostic: too strong (for every, not R)

truefeedback.text: Assuming that {@dtarel@} holds for every choice is far more than the statement being false. A ‘for every’ statement is false as soon as one choice fails it.

[[if test='tstrict']]Your inequality includes the case where the two sides are equal. That case agrees with the statement, {@dtorig@}, so it is not part of its negation.[[else]]Your inequality leaves out the case where the two sides are equal. In that case the statement, {@dtorig@}, is false, so that case belongs to its negation.[[/if]]

node.description: Diagnostic: right quantifier, inequality not the opposite

truefeedback.text: ‘At least one choice’ is right. But your inequality is not the opposite of {@dtorig@}: a choice that satisfies it need not contradict the statement.

falsefeedback.text: The statement says that every choice satisfies the inequality. For it to be false, how many choices have to fail? A choice fails the inequality exactly when the opposite inequality holds: \(\geq\) becomes \(\lt\), \(\gt\) becomes \(\leq\), \(\leq\) becomes \(\gt\), and \(\lt\) becomes \(\geq\).
